qualifications.text:
Point 6 The bill gives one U.S. state's supervision nationwide reach with only a conditional federal backup.

  • Because “The bill would permit a nonbank issuer with under $10 billion in outstanding stablecoins to opt in to a state regulatory regime and operate nationally.” [25]
  • Because A federal waiver can keep larger issuers in that system too. Section 4(d)(3) allows an issuer “with a consolidated total outstanding issuance of more than $10,000,000,000 to remain solely supervised by a State payment stablecoin regulator.” [4]
  • Because That makes the resources of the home-state supervisor matter across the country. CRS identifies the concern that state regulators lack “supervisory resources comparable to federal ones.” [2] CRS is the Congressional Research Service, which does research for Congress.
  • Because Without an agreement allowing routine Federal Reserve participation, section 7's emergency enforcement route for the Federal Reserve and Comptroller requires “unusual and exigent circumstances” [4] and “not less than 48 hours' prior written notice to the applicable State payment stablecoin regulator” [4]. The clause for each regulator is “Subject to subparagraph (C)” [4], which lets these regulators restrict an issuer by directive after finding a serious risk during those circumstances. The bill's text does not separately state a notice period for those directives. This backup is a new federal power, so the concern is not that the bill reduces existing federal authority. The concern is that national reach raises the stakes of these limits.
  • Note Certifying that a state's rules are “substantially similar to the Federal regulatory framework under this Act” [4] does not supply equal staffing or remove the federal notice requirement.
  • So A failure of local supervision can expose payments nationwide while the new federal backup is limited by these conditions and can face a notice period. Giving national reach to that weak point can strain the federal government's ability to contain a fast threat.

qualifications.text:
Point 6 The bill gives one U.S. state's supervision nationwide reach with only a conditional federal backup.

  • Because “The bill would permit a nonbank issuer with under $10 billion in outstanding stablecoins to opt in to a state regulatory regime and operate nationally.” [25]
  • Because A federal waiver can keep larger issuers in that system too. Section 4(d)(3) allows an issuer “with a consolidated total outstanding issuance of more than $10,000,000,000 to remain solely supervised by a State payment stablecoin regulator.” [4]
  • Because That makes the resources of the home-state supervisor matter across the country. CRS identifies the concern that state regulators lack “supervisory resources comparable to federal ones.” [2] CRS is the Congressional Research Service, which does research for Congress.
  • Because Without an agreement allowing routine Federal Reserve participation, section 7's emergency enforcement route for the Federal Reserve and Comptroller requires “unusual and exigent circumstances” [4] and “not less than 48 hours' prior written notice to the applicable State payment stablecoin regulator” [4]. The clause for each regulator is “Subject to subparagraph (C)” [4], which lets these regulators restrict an issuer by directive after finding a serious risk during those circumstances. The bill's text does not separately state a notice period for those directives. This backup is a new federal power, so the concern is not that the bill reduces existing federal authority. The concern is that national reach raises the stakes of these limits.
  • Note Certifying that a state's rules are “substantially similar to the Federal regulatory framework under this Act” [4] does not supply equal staffing or remove the federal notice requirement.
  • So A failure of local supervision can expose payments nationwide while the new federal backup is limited by these conditions and can face a notice period. Giving national reach to that weak point can strain the federal government's ability to contain a fast threat.

Brief context note: The 2026 Trade Policy Agenda (March 2026) comes from the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR), the U.S. trade agency. The agenda lists labor and environmental standards and national and economic security among the commitments in Agreements on Reciprocal Trade (ARTs), which are trade deals. It describes each ART as requiring the United States to maintain a modified tariff (an added tariff above the normal rate). USTR says courts can review the tools for maintaining those tariffs and that those tools may change. USTR also says it expects to keep working with partners to implement the deals, and that it will closely monitor implementation and enforce when necessary. The agenda names Cambodia and Malaysia as signed ARTs and Thailand as a framework deal. This is official U.S. intention from after the bill date, when replacement tariffs applied. The agenda reports no foreign compliance and no labor or environmental result. It also does not test a hypothetical repeal on October 30, 2025. Sources: [34].

Brief context note: On February 21, 2026, Malaysia's trade ministry said Malaysia had signed its Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (ART) with the United States but had not ratified it (given it final legal approval). The ministry said Malaysia was assessing recent U.S. legal and policy developments. The statement recognized that the United States retains other legal mechanisms to impose tariffs and noted a temporary 10% tariff. The statement reports no withdrawal, termination or implementation result. This setting, with replacement tariffs, differs from the comparison used here: ending the emergency on October 30, 2025. Sources: [35].

Evidence note: On October 22, 2025, Malaysia's trade minister said of Lynas: "We will not stop them from exporting to markets of their choice," naming South Korea, Japan and the United States. Malaysia separately has a moratorium on exporting unprocessed rare earths. Lynas said in May it was engaged with customers in Japan, the United States and Europe. The sources reviewed identify no restriction under consideration for this supply. Sources: [45], [43].

Response The PRO leaves out the link between issuer cash-out terms and the terms for spending money held through other firms.

  • Because Section 4 regulates “the issuer's redemption policy” [3]. The 7-day notice is the issuer's duty.
  • Because A prospectus that the stablecoin issuer Circle published before the vote explains: “Transactions between third parties may be subject to fees charged by the parties to the transaction or the secondary marketplace on which the transaction occurs.” [9] Those fees and terms “are governed by agreements between the parties to the transactions and/or the rules of the secondary marketplace” [9]. The secondary market is where people trade coins with each other, not with the issuer.
  • So This response does not dispute the protection for people who redeem directly with an issuer. The response challenges the wider step: the issuer's notice does not govern the charges and delays of every wallet, exchange, or cash-pickup firm. The PRO has not shown how the change improves access for households relying on those firms.

Response The PRO's Celsius example does not show the added protection it is used to illustrate.

  • Because The cited harm concerns “major crypto platforms such as Celsius and Voyager” [6]. A report about a coin issuer's reserves is not a report about a separate platform's ability to return its customers' money.
  • Because The FDIC stated in 2022: “The Federal Deposit Insurance Act (FDI Act) prohibits any person from representing or implying that an uninsured product is FDIC–insured or from knowingly misrepresenting the extent and manner of deposit insurance.” [12] So the deposit-insurance part of the bill's marketing ban overlaps an existing prohibition. FDIC is the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation.
  • So This response does not answer the bill's reserve reports, executive certifications, and ban on claims of U.S. government backing. The Celsius example does not establish how those provisions relieve customers of judging the safety of a separate platform holding their savings.

Response The protection the PRO describes when a firm fails does not reach Treasury reserves that a lender can take first.

A lender can take Treasury reserves first. Section 4 permits using Treasury reserves as collateral for borrowing to meet redemptions: “creating liquidity to meet reasonable expectations of requests to redeem payment stablecoins” [UNC 3]. Brookings explains these secured loans, called repurchase agreements or repo: in bankruptcy, “the repo lender could seize the Treasury collateral if the stablecoin issuer could not return the cash.” [UNC 13] Then “assets in segregated accounts would fall short of what is needed for 1:1 redemption.” [UNC 13] A right to share those assets does not restore the seized collateral. Brookings is a policy research group.

  • So This response does not answer the protection against other business debts. The response challenges the PRO's description of holders' claim to a full proportionate share of reserves where reserves have been pledged as collateral to a lender.

Response The PRO's examples do not establish that larger credits add abuse or victim debts under the rules in force on January 8.

  • Because GAO tested failures in enrollment checks, not how abuse changes with credit amounts. It warns: “The results of our covert testing, while illustrative of potential enrollment control weaknesses, cannot be generalized to the overall enrollment population.” [30]

  • Because The December report in the PRO finds unauthorized plan switching mainly in the federal enrollment system.   • Because The PRO's larger-debt claim depends on an ineligible enrollment remaining uncorrected. The agency running the federal Marketplace (CMS) has an established process for correcting unauthorized coverage and its tax records: “These actions include retroactively restoring or cancelling coverage and updating tax forms to ensure consumers do not suffer adverse tax implications when unauthorized activity occurs.” [36] A comparison of victim debts must account for those corrections.
  • So Gaps in those check calls and the blocked five-dollar charge identify failures in safeguards. They do not establish the added harm from changing credit amounts. This response does not answer the reporting that plans with no monthly bill make an unwanted enrollment harder to notice. It limits how far the PRO's examples and repayment figure can show added harm under the rules in force.

The review cited by the PRO says hormone-naive transgender women (those who have not taken hormone treatment) may not on average have the same athletic attributes as cisgender men. Evidence note: The McNabb injury occurred on September 1, 2022. North Carolina's state ban took effect August 16, 2023 and applied from the 2023-2024 school year. Sources: [14], [17].

Evidence note: Snopes, a fact-checking website, states in March 2025 that it is not possible to verify whether the player who spiked the ball into Payton McNabb's head was transgender. It also states that a volleyball player can sustain such injuries regardless of opponents' gender identity. Snopes also reports three more things. The school board's notes described an opposing athlete as transgender without providing evidence. The board stopped games amid safety concerns from some parents and players, while several coaches spoke for continuing. North Carolina's association approved two transgender girls from 2019 to 2023, and their sports are unclear. Rep. Harris told the House a "teenage boy" spiked the ball. North Carolina's state ban applied from the 2023-2024 school year. Sources: [15], [2], [18].

Evidence note: A 2026 British Journal of Sports Medicine systematic review (52 studies) reports pooled comparisons of transgender women and cisgender women as similar on relative lean mass, upper-body and lower-body strength and maximal oxygen consumption. The statistical ranges for those comparisons include zero (no difference), and certainty is rated low or very low. Its conclusion states higher lean mass with comparable fitness and calls the evidence mostly low certainty. A later correction removed three studies, added one and said the main conclusions were unchanged. These are averages for body composition and fitness. The text in this project's evidence collection reports no result by sport for absolute mass, speed, collisions or injuries. Only the abstract and correction notice are in this collection, so the review's full methods were not verified. The review came after the comparison date but before the evidence cutoff. Sources: [8], [9].

Evidence note: Federal Reserve Governor Waller describes limited use of stablecoins by ordinary customers (retail use) and says a significant retail impact would probably take years. They do not by themselves refute the PRO's conditional exposure route: if more households use these coins, more households face these risks. Sources: [25], [23], [26].

The ministry said Malaysia was assessing recent U.S. legal and policy developments. The statement recognized that the United States retains other legal mechanisms to impose tariffs and noted a temporary 10% tariff. The statement reports no withdrawal, termination or implementation result. This setting, with replacement tariffs, differs from the comparison used here: ending the emergency on October 30, 2025. Sources: [35].

On October 22, 2025, Malaysia's trade minister said of Lynas: "We will not stop them from exporting to markets of their choice," naming South Korea, Japan and the United States. Malaysia separately has a moratorium on exporting unprocessed rare earths. Lynas said in May it was engaged with customers in Japan, the United States and Europe. The sources reviewed identify no restriction under consideration for this supply. Sources: [45], [43].

Reported changes were partial. Tom Homan, a top administration official on border policy, said people in the country illegally are “not off the table” [15], even if they were not the original targets. Chicago volunteers said “people who weren’t the original targets but are nearby might also get arrested.” [28] One immigration-restriction advocate said of the change: “it’s not clear this means they’re actually stepping back from immigration.” [26] Human Rights Watch says the package moves “without adopting essential oversight and accountability reforms.” [27]

patches.after:
Reports before Congress's June 9 vote described changes in how agents made arrests: more targeted arrests and fewer large, visible sweeps. These reports also show limits to the changes. Tom Homan, a top administration official on border policy, said immigration agents would keep arresting people they find during operations if those people are in the country illegally. This includes people with no criminal history who were not the original targets. He said such people are “not off the table” [15], meaning agents can still arrest them. Cristóbal Cavazos, who leads a workers center near Chicago, said he has seen as many as seven agents trying to arrest one person. WBEZ reported that this means “people who weren’t the original targets but are nearby might also get arrested.” [28] Mark Krikorian, who leads a group that advocates for immigration restrictions, said the Trump administration had clearly stepped back from its earlier tactics. He then said: “it’s not clear this means they’re actually stepping back from immigration.” [26] Here “they” means the Trump administration. Human Rights Watch said on June 16 that Congress approved S.2 “without adopting essential oversight and accountability reforms.” [27] Lawmakers and activists had proposed reforms such as requiring warrants from judges and stronger bans on racial profiling.

  • Because Human Rights Watch found federal agents in Los Angeles “detaining people based on their perceived race, ethnicity, or national origin” [19].

Point 1 Required backing protects money that people with little financial cushion need for essentials.

  • Because Issuers licensed under the bill must keep reserves worth at least the full amount they owe users. See C04.
  • Because Reuse is limited to listed reserve-investment, custody, and cash-out needs. Outside those purposes, reserves “may not be pledged, rehypothecated, or reused by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, either directly or indirectly” [3]. To rehypothecate means to reuse an asset as security for a loan.
  • Because Safe, readily available backing supports repayment: “they need to be backed by safe and liquid assets, like cash, Treasury bills, and central bank reserves, so they can offer convertibility at par.” [5] At par means at the full promised value.
  • Because Ordinary crypto users are less able to absorb losses: “most retail participants lack the resources, information, and financial resilience needed to navigate this volatile space.” [6]
  • Because Dollar-linked coins also serve people facing unstable currencies: “Stablecoins can also mitigate local currency and inflationary risks, major advantages in volatile markets.” [7]
  • Because Aid recipients already use them. UNHCR “successfully executed a small pilot to distribute cash assistance to a group of people displaced by the war in Ukraine in Circle Internet Financial’s USD Coin (USDC)” [8].
  • So Enforceable backing rules protect against coins issued without enough money to repay users. That protects small savings and aid payments, including money vulnerable people abroad need for food, shelter, and care.

Point 1 It strengthens the state’s tools for finding and cutting off funds for terrorists, cartels, and other security threats.

  • Because Stablecoins already serve these threats: “Evidence points to increased use for terrorist financing and money laundering.” [3]
  • Because Permitted issuers must check their account holders and report suspicious transactions: “identification and verification of account holders with the permitted payment stablecoin issuer” [4]. The reporting duty is in C27, and whether it helps identify payments is in C18.
  • Because Issuers must certify programs aimed at preventing “facilitating money laundering for cartels and organizations designated as foreign terrorist organizations” [4]. Failure to submit the certification lets regulators “revoke the approval of the payment stablecoin issuer under this section.” [4]
  • Because The bill bars officers and directors convicted of felonies involving “cybercrime, money laundering, financing of terrorism, or financial fraud” [4]. Federal licensing also weighs the “competence, experience, and integrity of the officers, directors, and principal shareholders” [4].
  • Because It makes the ability and willingness to obey federal blocking orders a condition of issuance. See C13.
  • Because Treasury can act against foreign issuers that defy those orders, after notice. See C14.
  • Because The foreign-issuer registration review checks “whether the foreign payment stablecoin issuer presents illicit finance risks to the United States.” [4] Registered issuers must “consent to United States jurisdiction relating to the enforcement of this Act.” [4]
  • Because That foreign-issuer route excludes countries under sweeping U.S. sanctions or designated as major money-laundering risks: the country must be “not subject to comprehensive economic sanctions by the United States or in a jurisdiction that the Secretary of the Treasury has determined to be a jurisdiction of primary money laundering concern.” [4]
  • Because Treasury must research better detection methods, and its financial-crime agency must issue guidance and rules on monitoring blockchain transfers. See C19. Some services can hide who sends or receives money.
  • So Licensing checks, reporting, blocking technology, and access to U.S. trading platforms give the state ways to trace and interrupt threat financing. Better detection rules extend those defenses as methods change. That strengthens the country's ability to protect its citizens.

patches.after: The April 2026 proposed rule from FinCEN and OFAC would apply duties in the secondary market (trades between other people, not with the issuer) to blocking, freezing and rejecting impermissible transactions and to complying with lawful orders. FinCEN is Treasury's financial-crime agency. OFAC is the Office of Foreign Assets Control, which enforces U.S. sanctions. Sources: [6].
